gendered_labor.assessment: No Yolŋu-specific quantitative ethnography of subsistence division was located in this research pass beyond the general Aboriginal-Australia pattern (men typically hunting larger/mobile game, women gathering plant foods and smaller game, with documented cross-cultural exceptions in other groups). Flagged as a gap requiring further targeted search rather than asserted with confidence.

sources.citation: General Aboriginal-Australia subsistence-division literature; no Yolŋu-specific citation confirmed in this pass.

political_inequality.assessment: Age-and-gender-stratified, not a simple male/female hierarchy. Ian Keen, Knowledge and Secrecy in an Aboriginal Religion (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1994): senior men controlled secret religious knowledge (songs, stories, sacred objects), the basis of their authority over both women and junior men — a gerontocratic-patriarchal structure. Ian Keen, "How Some Murngin Men Marry Ten Wives," Man (N.S.) 17(4) (1982): 620-642, and John F. Martin and P. Govinda Reddy, "Gidjingali and Yolngu Polygyny: Age Structure and the Control of Marriage," Oceania 57(4) (1987): 243-260, document large husband-wife age gaps and marriages arranged for girls, often before puberty, controlled by senior men.

sources.citation: Keen, Ian. Knowledge and Secrecy in an Aboriginal Religion: Yolngu of North-East Arnhem Land. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1994.
sources.author: Ian Keen

sources.citation: Martin, John F., and P. Govinda Reddy. "Gidjingali and Yolngu Polygyny: Age Structure and the Control of Marriage." Oceania 57(4), 1987: 243-260.
sources.author: Martin and Reddy

legal_economic_status.assessment: Land/sea estate ownership (bäpurru) is vested in patrilineal clans; women are members of their father's clan/estate by birth. Specific documented content of women's independent proprietary/economic standing within that system was not pinned to a specific citation in this research pass — Nancy M. Williams, The Yolngu and Their Land: A System of Land Tenure and the Fight for Its Recognition (Canberra: AIAS, 1986), is very likely on-point but gender-specific content could not be extracted via search in this pass.

sources.citation: Williams, Nancy M. The Yolngu and Their Land: A System of Land Tenure and the Fight for Its Recognition. Canberra: AIAS, 1986 — existence/scope confirmed, gender-specific content not extracted this pass.
sources.author: Nancy M. Williams

household_authority.assessment: One tertiary (non-peer-reviewed) source describes polygynous households as layered: co-wives may live in separate dwellings with a senior wife as head of her own household, while the husband is regarded as head across all his households. Treat as UNKNOWN pending primary-source confirmation.

sources.citation: Tertiary secondary-source characterization of Yolŋu polygynous household structure, not traced to a named academic publication in this pass.

gendered_legal_restrictions.assessment: A formal, named, gender-differentiated restriction regime ("men's business"/"women's business") structures the entire ceremonial-knowledge system — the central subject of Keen (1994). This is corroborated by a positively-documented, distinct women's ceremonial sphere (not merely exclusion from men's ceremony) — see ideological_patriarchy below.

sources.citation: Keen, Ian. Knowledge and Secrecy in an Aboriginal Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1994.
sources.author: Ian Keen

ideological_patriarchy.assessment: DISPUTED, with two identifiable positions. [COMPLEMENTARITY school, associated with Diane Bell and the Kaberry-Hamilton-Bell tradition — Central Australian, NOT Yolŋu-specific fieldwork, should not be imported as a Yolŋu finding without this caveat]: separate men's and women's ritual domains constitute genuine interdependent, non-hierarchical spheres, with settlement/mission life (not precolonial tradition) as the primary driver of later female subordination. [GERONTOCRATIC-PATRIARCHAL school, Ian Keen's Yolŋu-specific analysis]: secrecy and control of sacred knowledge functioned specifically to entrench senior men's authority over both women and junior men — a real, documented power asymmetry co-existing with a distinct women's ceremonial sphere, not a fully symmetrical complementarity. Fiona Magowan, Melodies of Mourning: Music and Emotion in Northern Australia (Oxford: James Currey/Crawley: UWA Press, 2007), and "Shadows of Song: Exploring Research and Performance Strategies in Yolngu Women's Crying-Songs," Oceania 72(2) (2001): 89-104, documents women's "crying songs" as a domain where women hold, transmit, and control specific ritual/musical knowledge with real ceremonial authority — a positively-documented sphere, not an absence.

sources.citation: Keen, Ian. Knowledge and Secrecy in an Aboriginal Religion. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1994.
sources.author: Ian Keen

sources.citation: Magowan, Fiona. "Shadows of Song: Exploring Research and Performance Strategies in Yolngu Women's Crying-Songs." Oceania 72(2), 2001: 89-104.
sources.author: Fiona Magowan

dimensions.notes: Descent/land affiliation (patrifiliation to clan/moiety/estate) is a separate axis from gendered political authority — documented HIGH confidence, but does not by itself settle any of the six dimensions above, each independently evidenced. Required does_not_demonstrate: neither Magowan's documentation of positive women's ceremonial authority nor Keen's documentation of senior-male control of secret knowledge, alone, proves a whole-society verdict of "patriarchal" or "egalitarian" — both are separately true and documented, held side by side rather than collapsed.
